questions.questionText: According to the chapter, what is the defining feature of a first-story opener?
options: It opens with the speaker's emotional account of what happened before inviting the other person to respond
It treats the speaker's version of events as the baseline and positions the other person to respond to that assessment
It assigns explicit blame to one party before dialogue begins
It frames the disagreement as a problem that requires immediate resolution
questions.explanation: The chapter defines the first-story opener as starting from the speaker's own story — treating their version of events as the baseline — which places the other person in the role of defendant before any exchange has occurred. Their only options are to confirm, dispute, or defend against an assessment already made.

distractorNotes.0: Focusing on emotional experience is not the defining feature; the issue is that the speaker's interpretation of the situation is treated as established fact before the other person has said a word.
distractorNotes.1: Correct. The implicit premise of the first-story opener is: I have already assessed this situation, and you are being asked to respond to my assessment.
distractorNotes.2: First-story openers often contain no explicit blame — the chapter notes this is a structural problem, not a tonal one. A gentler first-story opener is still a first-story opener.
distractorNotes.3: Framing for resolution is not what distinguishes the first-story opener; the issue is starting from an already-established interpretation, not from a desire for resolution.

questions.questionText: The chapter identifies three things the third-story opener does. Which of the following is one of them?
options: It gives the speaker a structured way to rehearse their position before the conversation begins
It prevents the other person from raising concerns the speaker has not anticipated
It signals that the speaker has already researched both sides of the disagreement
It lowers the identity stakes by framing the situation so neither party is positioned as the one who got it wrong
questions.explanation: The chapter names three effects of the third-story opener: it does not assume the speaker is already right, it invites joint inquiry rather than message delivery, and it lowers the identity stakes — when no fault is assigned in the opening, neither party is positioned as the one who got it wrong.

distractorNotes.0: The third-story opener is not about rehearsing a position; it is about genuinely opening the situation to inquiry, which requires that the speaker not be privately certain they are right.
distractorNotes.1: The chapter does not claim the third-story opener forecloses what the other person can raise. Joint inquiry means both parties contribute what they see.
distractorNotes.2: Researching both sides is not part of the chapter's description of the third-story opener or its effects.
distractorNotes.3: Correct. The chapter explicitly names lowering identity stakes as one of the three things the shift accomplishes.

questions.questionText: The chapter says the first-story opener triggers defensiveness for structural reasons, not tonal ones. What does this mean?
options: The implicit premise of the opener treats the speaker's interpretation as already established, leaving the other person no role except to confirm, dispute, or defend against an assessment already made
The tone of difficult conversations is inherently adversarial because of the high stakes involved for both parties
First-story openers always contain accusatory language even when the speaker believes they are being neutral
The other person's identity is directly threatened by the subject matter of most difficult conversations, regardless of how the opener is framed
questions.explanation: The chapter distinguishes between tone and structure. A gentle first-story opener is still a first-story opener. Defenses come up not because of how the speaker sounds, but because of the implicit premise: the speaker has already assessed the situation and is asking the other person to respond to that assessment.

distractorNotes.0: Correct. This is the structural problem the chapter names: the opener's implicit premise, not its wording or delivery, is what forces the other person into a defensive position.
distractorNotes.1: The chapter does not characterize difficult conversations as inherently adversarial — it argues that how they are opened determines the stance, and the stance can be changed.
distractorNotes.2: The chapter explicitly says a gentler first-story opener is still a first-story opener — it is not that the language is always accusatory; it is that the structure positions one party's interpretation as baseline.
distractorNotes.3: While identity stakes are a real factor in difficult conversations, the chapter's point here is about the structure of the opener specifically, not about the subject matter creating unavoidable defensiveness.

questions.questionText: The chapter distinguishes between an invitation and a summons at the close of a third-story opener. What is the operational difference?
options: An invitation always uses question form; a summons uses declarative statements regardless of how they are phrased
An invitation omits any mention of the speaker's own concerns; a summons foregrounds them at the outset
An invitation signals the speaker genuinely expects to learn something from the conversation; a summons closes inquiry even when the opening is neutrally framed
An invitation is appropriate in personal relationships; a summons is the correct form in professional contexts
questions.explanation: The chapter makes this distinction when describing Tsega's rewrite: 'I'd like to get clearer on that' signals she has something to learn from the conversation. The chapter warns that a neutrally framed opener that closes with 'I need you to understand why this is a problem' has not made the full move — the frame and the invitation belong together.

distractorNotes.0: The chapter does not define the distinction by grammatical form. A question can still close inquiry if it embeds an assumption; a declarative can invite genuine exploration.
distractorNotes.1: The chapter does not say the speaker must omit their concerns. The third-story opener names the disagreement — the key is how the opener positions the other person's view.
distractorNotes.2: Correct. The invitation signals that hearing the other person's view is part of why the speaker is raising the issue — not a courtesy, but a genuine purpose of the conversation.
distractorNotes.3: The chapter draws no distinction between personal and professional contexts here. The invitation/summons distinction applies wherever a third-story opener is used.

questions.questionText: Soren has written two drafts of a message to Claudia about mid-sprint requirements changes. Draft A: 'I need to flag a concern about how mid-sprint requirements changes are being handled — it's been creating significant rework and I think we need a different process.' Draft B: 'I think we've been working from different assumptions about what should trigger a mid-sprint change, and I'd like to compare notes so we're starting from the same place.' Which is the third-story opener, and why?
options: Draft A, because it uses 'I' statements that center the speaker's experience rather than accusing Claudia directly
Draft B, because it frames the issue as a gap in shared assumptions rather than treating Soren's interpretation as already established
Draft A, because it identifies a concrete problem that needs solving rather than leaving the situation vague
Both are third-story openers because neither names Claudia as personally responsible for the rework
questions.explanation: The chapter uses this exact pair to illustrate the difference. Draft A treats Soren's interpretation as the baseline — here is what happened, here is why it is a problem, now respond. Draft B frames the situation as a gap between assumptions: neither party has been adjudicated as wrong, and Claudia's view is something Soren has not yet heard. The chapter notes: 'The first message treats Claudia as someone who needs to receive a concern. The second treats her as someone whose view Soren has not yet heard.'

distractorNotes.0: Using 'I' statements does not make an opener a third-story opener. Draft A's 'I' framing still treats Soren's account as the established baseline. The structural problem is not in the subject of the sentence.
distractorNotes.1: Correct. Draft B names a gap in assumptions — an account that belongs to neither party — and closes with an invitation to compare notes rather than a conclusion already reached.
distractorNotes.2: Identifying a concrete problem is not the criterion. Draft A's concreteness is part of how it presents the speaker's interpretation as established fact.
distractorNotes.3: Draft A positions Claudia as someone who needs to respond to a concern Soren has already assessed. The third-story opener names the disagreement without assigning it to anyone's failure; Draft A does not do this.

questions.questionText: A colleague wants to raise a recurring concern about how client handoffs are being managed. Which of the following responses best follows the chapter's guidance for a third-story opener?
options: 'I want to be upfront: the way you've been handling client handoffs has been adding to my workload, and I need that to change.'
'I don't want this to become a big thing, but I've been frustrated about how the handoffs have been going.'
'I know you're probably not aware, but the current handoff process isn't working for me or the team.'
'I think we might be operating with different expectations about how handoffs are supposed to work — I'd like to get us on the same page.'
questions.explanation: Option D names the gap between expectations — an account that belongs to neither party — and closes with a genuine invitation ('I'd like to get us on the same page') that signals the speaker expects to hear the other person's view. The other options each start from the speaker's story and place the colleague in the role of defendant.

distractorNotes.0: This is a direct first-story opener: it names a conclusion already reached ('the way you've been handling') and closes with a demand. It may be appropriate in some contexts, but it is not a third-story opener.
distractorNotes.1: Softening the tone ('I don't want this to become a big thing') does not change the structure. The speaker is still starting from their own frustration as the baseline.
distractorNotes.2: The opener embeds an assessment ('not working for me or the team') before the other person has spoken, and 'I know you're probably not aware' implies the speaker already knows what the other person doesn't. This is a first-story opener with a softer register.
distractorNotes.3: Correct. This frames the disagreement as a gap in shared expectations — neither party has been assigned the wrong view — and invites joint inquiry.

questions.questionText: A manager uses a third-story opener to begin a performance conversation: 'I think we might be seeing this quarter's targets differently — I'd like to hear your read before we compare notes.' The employee still becomes defensive and asks, 'So you're saying I missed my targets?' What is the most likely explanation according to the chapter?
options: The manager wrote a neutrally framed opener but remained privately certain the employee missed targets, so the invitation was not genuine — the employee could sense the frame was being used rather than meant
The employee's identity stakes were unusually high and no conversational framing could have prevented a defensive response
The third-story opener is only effective when both parties have agreed in advance to use the framework
The manager did not leave enough time between sending the message and beginning the conversation for the opener to land correctly
questions.explanation: The chapter explicitly addresses this: 'A third-story opener delivered while remaining privately certain you are right uses the form without the stance.' The chapter goes further: this can function as manipulation, 'more corrosive than an honest first-story opener, because it obscures the speaker's actual intent while appearing fair-minded.' If the invitation is not genuine, the other person usually senses it.

distractorNotes.0: Correct. The chapter locates the failure in the speaker's internal stance, not in the framing itself. A form without the stance can be more corrosive than a direct first-story opener.
distractorNotes.1: The chapter does not characterize defensiveness as unavoidable based on identity-stake levels. It treats defensiveness as a signal about what the opener communicated — explicitly or implicitly.
distractorNotes.2: The chapter makes no requirement for prior agreement on the framework. The third-story opener is presented as something one party can initiate.
distractorNotes.3: Timing of message delivery is not addressed in the chapter's account of why the third-story opener misfires.

questions.questionText: A manager opens a feedback conversation: 'I've noticed a pattern in how you've been interacting with the team during standups. I want to understand what's behind it.' How should this opener be classified, and why?
options: Third-story opener, because the manager asks a question rather than stating a conclusion about the employee's behavior
Third-story opener, because the manager frames the situation as a pattern across time rather than pointing to a single incident
First-story opener, because the manager has already named the observation as established ('a pattern') and positioned the employee to explain behavior the manager has already assessed
Cannot be determined without knowing the tone and relationship context in which it was delivered
questions.explanation: The manager's opener embeds an assessment — 'a pattern' — before any exchange. The employee is invited not to jointly examine what happened but to explain themselves in relation to a conclusion already reached. The question 'I want to understand what's behind it' does not open the frame; it calls for the employee to account for a situation the manager has already interpreted.

distractorNotes.0: Ending with a question does not make the opener a third-story opener if the question invites explanation of an already-named assessment. The question here asks 'what is behind' a 'pattern' the manager has declared.
distractorNotes.1: Referencing a pattern rather than a single incident does not change the structure. The chapter's distinction is about whether the speaker's interpretation is treated as established — and here, 'a pattern' does exactly that.
distractorNotes.2: Correct. 'I've noticed a pattern' establishes the manager's interpretation as the baseline. 'I want to understand what's behind it' then asks the employee to account for something the manager has already concluded. This is a first-story opener in a gentler register.
distractorNotes.3: The chapter specifically argues that the structural problem is not tonal — a gentler first-story opener is still a first-story opener. Tone and relationship context do not determine which story the opener belongs to.

questions.questionText: The chapter names two things the third-story opener cannot fix. A team lead uses a third-story opener with a direct report who has just come from a difficult client call. The direct report says, 'Can you just — I need a minute. I'm not ready to problem-solve yet.' Which of the chapter's named limits does this illustrate?
options: The structural power gap: when significant authority differentials exist, joint inquiry is nominal in a way both parties sense

The acknowledgment-before-inquiry limit: when one person genuinely needs to feel heard before any exploration is possible, a third-story opener can feel evasive — procedurally correct but relationally wrong
The factual dispute limit: when the disagreement involves demonstrable facts rather than interpretations, the third-story frame cannot bridge the difference
The written communication limit: the third-story opener only works reliably in face-to-face contexts where tone can be calibrated in real time
questions.explanation: The chapter names this condition explicitly: 'Some conversations involve a genuine need to feel heard before exploration is possible. A third-story opener in those situations can feel evasive — procedurally correct but relationally wrong, more interested in being fair-minded than in understanding what the other person has been through.' The direct report is not ready for joint inquiry; they need acknowledgment first.

distractorNotes.0: The power-gap limit is the second thing the chapter names, but it refers to situations where the underlying authority structure determines the outcome regardless of framing — not to a situation where the employee signals they need to be heard before problem-solving.
distractorNotes.1: Correct. The direct report's response ('I need a minute — I'm not ready to problem-solve yet') is exactly the signal the chapter describes: acknowledgment must come before inquiry for this conversation to go anywhere.
distractorNotes.2: The chapter does not name factual disputes as one of the two limits of the third-story opener. The framework is about interpretations and assumptions, but the chapter does not exclude factual disagreements from its scope.
distractorNotes.3: The chapter does not restrict the third-story opener to face-to-face contexts. Soren's opener is delivered in writing.

questions.questionText: A project manager sits down to write a third-story opener to a colleague about a missed deadline. As she drafts the neutral frame, she notices the phrasing feels dishonest — 'I know exactly what happened here, and pretending I don't feels wrong.' According to the chapter, what does this feeling indicate?
options: She is not yet skilled enough at the framing to write the opener convincingly and needs more practice before attempting it
The situation is genuinely too one-sided for the third-story frame to apply — some situations really do have a clear account
She should acknowledge her own view explicitly at the start to avoid appearing manipulative
The learning stance is not genuinely in place — she is still privately certain she is right, and the neutral frame feels dishonest because it does not reflect how she actually sees the situation
questions.explanation: The chapter addresses this directly: 'If writing the neutral opener feels dishonest — if it feels like pretending not to know something you already know — the question is not how to phrase the opening. It is whether the learning stance is actually in place.' The feeling of dishonesty is a signal about her internal stance, not a problem with the technique.

distractorNotes.0: The chapter does not attribute this feeling to a skill deficit. The issue is not that she cannot write the framing — it is that her internal stance does not match what the framing implies.
distractorNotes.1: The chapter does not carve out 'genuinely one-sided' situations as exceptions to the third-story opener. It locates the source of the feeling of dishonesty in the speaker's own privately-held certainty, not in the objective nature of the dispute.
distractorNotes.2: The chapter does not recommend starting with the speaker's own view as an alternative when the third-story opener feels dishonest. It points inward: the question is whether genuine openness is in place, not how to phrase the opener differently.
distractorNotes.3: Correct. The chapter is explicit: the feeling of dishonesty when writing the opener is a diagnostic signal. It indicates that the speaker has not yet made the learning stance move — they are still privately certain they are right.
